name: Giog
description: Giog is a Malaysian multi-trick game played with Xiangqi pieces used like hidden cards, where players lead valid single or multi-piece combinations and capture tricks with the highest combination of the led type.
origin: Malaysia and Southeast Asian Chinese communities

history.origins: Giog is a Malaysian version of a game played with Chinese chess pieces used as playing-cards, with related forms across China and Southeast Asian Chinese communities.
timeline: Traditional era: Regional chess-piece trick games developed in Chinese communities.
2019: Detailed Giog and related-variant documentation published.
2024: Documentation updated with expanded variant references and details.
history.cultural: The game adapts the widely available Xiangqi piece set into a social competitive trick format.
history.evolution: Local variants differ in distribution method, valid combinations, tie handling, and scoring, while retaining hidden-piece trick capture structure.

setup.players: Base game is typically four players, with adapted procedures for three and two.
setup.deck: 32 Xiangqi pieces (16 red, 16 black) ranked from red general down to black pawn in base Giog.
setup.dealing: Pieces are mixed face down into paired stacks. Players reveal selected bottom pieces to establish priority order, then draft stacks around the layout to form hands (8 pieces each in four-player game).
setup.equipment: Xiangqi pieces and optional racks for concealed hand management.

rules.objective: Capture more pieces in tricks than opponents by winning leads with stronger valid combinations of matching type.
rules.gameplay: Priority-order first player leads to trick one; trick winner leads next. Leader plays one valid combination face down and others must play same number of pieces face down. After reveal, highest valid combination of the same type as the lead wins the trick and captures all played pieces. In base Giog, valid lead types are: single, identical pair, Giog noble triple family, Sam Mui (three soldiers/pawns), Si Mui (four soldiers/pawns), and Wu Mui (five soldiers/pawns). A general or marshal cannot be played in first or last trick ('beheading the cock'); violating this voids all captures by that player. For three-piece leads, leader must announce whether the type is Giog or Sam Mui, since only matching type can beat it.
keyRules: Other players may play any pieces of the required count, but only matching lead type can win.
Leader has priority in ties; otherwise tie breaks by earlier established player-priority order.
General/marshal are forbidden in first and last trick, including as part of combinations.
Hand ends when all pieces are played; player with most captured pieces wins in the base rule set.

strategy.basic: Preserve top-ranked control pieces for key leads and late-trick control, especially around first/last trick marshal restrictions.
strategy.intermediate: Track disclosed and inferred duplicates to judge when pair and soldier-set leads are likely unbeatable.
strategy.advanced: Use lead-type selection to force weak responses, especially by switching between single, pair, and announced three-piece families.
tips: When leading three pieces, announce type correctly because Giog and Sam Mui are not cross-comparable.
Priority order from distribution matters in tie cases where leader is not tied.

scoring.winCondition: Capture the highest number of pieces; ties for most are drawn/shared in the base rule.
